target_customer: Battery and EV makers that would license charging protocols and battery technology
problem: Lithium-ion batteries take long to charge and fast charging shortens cycle life.
business_model: Technology licensing and battery development for OEMs

founders.name: Tim Sherstyuk
education: Carleton University, chemistry program, dropped out
founders.background_notes: Globe and Mail (Jan 2015) states he was 21 then; not used as age at founding.

founders.name: Nick Sherstyuk
previous_startups: Family business in Ukraine (outcome not stated)
founders.background_notes: Electrical engineer and engineering entrepreneur, father of Tim Sherstyuk, per Globe and Mail.

founders.name: Kostyantyn Khomutov
founders.background_notes: Quoted as CEO in 2020 Ottawa Business Journal coverage; whether he co-founded at YC time is not established by opened sources.

technical_complexity.rationale: Battery management and charging control that must extend cycle life under fast charge is electrochemistry plus embedded algorithms; the 2019 claims drew skepticism from outlets.

defensibility.rationale: Proprietary charging algorithms and licensing model, but unverified performance claims and no sourced patents.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows an incumbent copying or buying the company; it remains independent per its website.

market_need_then: Laptop and phone battery life complaints drove the first product (Battery Box external battery) in 2014 and 2015. EV fast charging became the focus by 2019.

identity.logo: Wordmark; one source says Desk Sans typeface since about 2018

branding.community_and_virality: Press coverage in 2019 (TechCrunch, Axios, InsideEVs) was about the technology claims, not the brand.

brand_strength.rationale: No sourced evidence of brand pull; the name is generic battery wording.

pivots.from: Battery Box external battery for laptops and phones (planned 2015 launch)
pivots.to: EV ultra-fast charging protocol and later Li-metal cells
pivots.why: Not stated in sources; coverage shows the shift to EV charging at CES January 2019.

outcome_analysis: GBatteries is still operating. It began as a consumer battery accessory, took the YC seed in 2014, and re-emerged in 2019 with EV fast charging claims that outlets called promising but unproven. Documented funding is mostly Canadian public money in 2020, and no large venture round was verified, so its outcome remains open.
notes: Founder lineup differs by source (YC page lists Nick Sherstyuk; Solar Impulse lists Khomutov, Tim Sherstyuk, Tkachenko). Globe and Mail reported a seven-figure round in Jan 2015 without detail; not recorded as a round. Database totals (CB Insights 930K, Seedtable 912K) conflict and are unverified. Airbus Ventures, Initialized, SV Angel, Plug and Play reported as backers by profiles, round details unknown. 2020 grant is CAD 3 million (about USD 2.2M per S&P). No competitors were named in dated sources near the 2014 batch; the list is empty.
